title: Short Stuff: No Shirt, No Shoes, WTF
summary: Short Stuff episode on the "No Shirt, No Shoes, No Service" sign. Josh and Chuck discuss the history of the placards, which they say spread in the late 1960s and early 1970s as businesses tried to keep hippies out, though similar signs existed earlier in formal coastal Florida towns. They cite a researcher (William Roarer Baugh, per the transcript) and the Society for Barefoot Living, which wrote to state health departments and reported that no law bars customers based on attire. They explain that federal civil rights law (the 1964 Civil Rights Act, referred to as 1904 in the transcript) and the Americans with Disabilities Act bar exclusion based on protected characteristics, while dress codes applied evenly to everyone are generally allowed. The episode closes with off-topic talk about slippers, resort wear, and shoes for Bahamas restaurants.

segments.title: Origins of the placards and hippies
segments.summary: The hosts say the signs spread in popularity in the late 1960s and early 1970s in response to hippies. A researcher, William H. Roarer Ball, said the signs existed earlier but were mostly in formal coastal Florida towns in the 1950s.

segments.title: Health department letters and the law
segments.summary: The Society for Barefoot Living wrote to state health departments, which said no law bars customers from entering without shoes or a shirt. Health departments are concerned with employees, not customers.

segments.title: Civil rights law and dress codes
segments.summary: The hosts explain that federal civil rights law bars businesses from refusing service based on religion, race, color, or national origin, and the ADA extends protections to people with disabilities. A business can require attire if it applies to everyone and not just one protected group.
